sections.name: General Knowledge
sections.note: Part 1 (VALR, DM, QADI) shares a combined 170-minute limit; GK is a separate 10-minute section with no negative marking.

items.passage: Behavioural nudges promise change without coercion: place fruit at eye level, make saving the default, remind people of appointments by text. The results are real but modest. A nudge that lifts enrolment by a few percentage points is celebrated, yet the underlying structure that produced the problem remains untouched. Defaults help people who already want to save; they do little for people whose wages cannot cover rent. Reminders help the forgetful; they do not help those who cannot afford the treatment. The appeal of nudges is understandable. They are cheap, they avoid political fights, and they let policymakers claim progress without confronting powerful interests. But when nudges become a substitute for structural reform, they do quiet harm: they suggest the problem was individual behaviour all along, and they drain energy from harder changes. Nudges work best as complements, small helps layered onto serious policy. Used alone, they are a polite way of leaving the real problem in place.
items.question: The author's main criticism of nudges is that they
options: can substitute for structural reform and leave real problems untouched
items.explanation: The passage says results are real but modest, and the harm comes when nudges substitute for structural reform. It denies they never work, notes they are cheap, and defines them as change without coercion.

items.question: The example of saving defaults is used to show that
options: most people do not want to save
nudges help those who already want to save but not those who cannot afford to
items.explanation: The passage says defaults help people who already want to save and do little for people whose wages cannot cover rent. The other readings distort the example.

items.question: Why are nudges appealing to policymakers, according to the passage?
options: They are cheap and avoid political fights
They require no evidence to justify
They are popular with powerful interests
items.explanation: The passage lists cheapness, avoidance of political fights, and claiming progress without confronting powerful interests. It says they do not solve structural problems, and popularity with powerful interests is not the stated appeal.

items.question: The author would most likely describe a nudge-only policy on poverty as
options: a polite way of leaving the real problem in place
items.explanation: The closing sentence calls nudge-only use a polite way of leaving the real problem in place. It is not structural reform, an effective substitute, or coercive.

items.passage: Numbers carry an authority that words rarely match. A claim stated as 73 percent sounds precise, tested and true, even when the underlying survey was small, biased or badly worded. This authority is borrowed: it comes from the rigour of mathematics, not from the quality of the data. People transfer the certainty of arithmetic to the uncertainty of measurement, and in doing so they stop asking the questions that matter: who was counted, who was left out, what exactly was asked, and whether the number means what it seems to mean. The remedy is not to distrust all numbers, which would leave decisions to anecdote and instinct. It is to ask for the number behind the number: the sample, the definition, the margin of error, the comparison. A single percentage without context is a slogan. The same percentage with its method attached becomes evidence. The difference between the two is the difference between being impressed by numbers and being informed by them.
items.question: Why do numbers carry authority, according to the passage?
options: Because people transfer the certainty of arithmetic to uncertain measurement
items.explanation: The passage says people transfer the certainty of arithmetic to the uncertainty of measurement. It warns surveys may be small or biased, so rigour and accuracy are not assumed.

items.question: The phrase 'the number behind the number' refers to
options: a larger number that proves the first
the arithmetic used to calculate the percentage
the sample, definition, margin of error and comparison
a secret figure hidden by researchers
items.explanation: The passage defines it as the sample, the definition, the margin of error and the comparison. The other options are not the definition given.

items.question: The author recommends that readers should
options: ask for method and context before accepting a number
rely on anecdote and instinct instead
items.explanation: The remedy given is to ask for the number behind the number, not to distrust all numbers or rely on anecdote. Accepting at face value is what the passage criticises.

items.question: The distinction between a slogan and evidence, in the author's view, is
options: whether the number is presented with its method
whether the number is a percentage
whether the number comes from a survey
whether the number is large or small
items.explanation: The passage says a single percentage without context is a slogan, and the same percentage with its method attached becomes evidence. Size, survey origin and percentage form are not the distinction.

items.question: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'a blessing in disguise'.
options: A lucky accident with no downside
A fortunate event that looks bad at first
items.explanation: A blessing in disguise is something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good. A secret gift, a pure accident and a ceremony miss the key element of apparent misfortune turning fortunate.

items.question: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to bite the bullet'.
options: To endure something unpleasant with courage
items.explanation: To bite the bullet means to face something difficult or unpleasant bravely. It is not about eating, mistakes or refusal.

items.question: Which of the following is the best summary of the argument: 'Talent alone does not guarantee success; without practice, feedback and persistence, even the gifted plateau.'?
options: Success needs practice, feedback and persistence alongside talent
items.explanation: The argument says talent without practice, feedback and persistence leads to a plateau, so success needs those alongside talent. It does not say talent is irrelevant, that the gifted always succeed, or that practice alone guarantees success.

items.question: Premise: Every successful product launch in the firm involved early customer testing. Conclusion: Early customer testing guarantees a successful launch. The flaw is
options: Confusing a necessary condition with a sufficient one
items.explanation: Early testing being present in every success shows it may be necessary, not that it alone guarantees success. The argument confuses necessity with sufficiency rather than appealing to authority, emotion or personal attack.

items.question: Which statement weakens the claim 'Raising the minimum wage always reduces employment'?
options: Some workers earn above the minimum wage
One city raised its minimum wage and employment stayed stable
Wages are a cost to employers
Employment fell in a city that cut wages
items.explanation: A case where the wage rose and employment stayed stable directly counters the always claim. That wages are a cost and some earn above the minimum do not test the claim, and a fall after a cut points the other way.

items.question: Which statement strengthens the claim 'Regular feedback improves performance'?
options: A team that received weekly feedback improved faster than a similar team that received none
items.explanation: Faster improvement in the feedback team compared with a similar team without feedback directly supports the claim. Time cost, dislike and tools do not provide supporting evidence.

items.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to RESILIENT.
items.explanation: Resilient means able to recover quickly from difficulties, so adaptable and quick to recover is closest. Fragile and rigid are opposites, and passive describes inaction rather than recovery.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to VIGILANT.
items.explanation: Vigilant means keeping careful watch, so careless is the opposite. Watchful, alert and attentive are synonyms.

items.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to SCRUTINY.
items.explanation: Scrutiny means critical observation or close examination, so close examination is the synonym. A glance is brief, praise is approval, and neglect is the opposite of attention.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to HUMBLE.
items.explanation: Humble means having a modest view of one's importance, so arrogant is the opposite. Modest is a synonym, and polite and quiet describe different traits.

items.question: Fill in the blank: The auditor found several ______ in the accounts that required further investigation.
items.explanation: Differences between records that need investigation are discrepancies. Clarifications, agreements and confirmations all suggest consistency rather than problems to investigate.

items.question: Fill in the blank: The speaker's ______ delivery held the audience's attention for the full hour.
items.explanation: Holding attention for a full hour requires an engaging delivery. Monotonous, hesitant and muffled would lose attention rather than hold it.

items.question: Identify the grammatically correct sentence.
options: The data show a clear trends.
The datas shows a clear trend.
The data shows a clear trend.
The data showing a clear trend.
items.explanation: Data is treated as a singular mass noun in this usage and takes shows, and trend is singular after a. Datas is not a word, show with a singular subject is wrong, and the last option is a fragment with no main verb.

items.question: Identify the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Between you and I, the plan needs work.
Between you and me, the plan needs work.
Between you and myself, the plan needs work.
Between you and me, the plan need work.
items.explanation: Between is a preposition and takes the object pronoun me, not I or myself. The verb needs must agree with the singular plan, so the second sentence is the only correct one.

items.question: Arrange the sentences in logical order. (1) Demand for the product doubled within a year. (2) The firm opened a second plant to meet orders. (3) A small workshop launched a low-cost water filter. (4) Rural households adopted it quickly because it needed no electricity.
items.explanation: The launch in 3 comes first, adoption in 4 follows, demand doubling in 1 is the result, and opening a second plant in 2 is the response. Any order placing demand or expansion before the launch breaks chronology.

items.question: Which is the best title for a passage arguing that small daily habits compound into large change over years?
items.explanation: A passage on small daily habits compounding fits Small Steps, Large Change. Overnight success contradicts compounding, talent is not the theme, and dangers of routine misstates the positive argument.

items.question: A passage argues that banning a harmful product outright often creates a black market, while taxing and regulating it reduces harm more reliably. The author's stance is best described as
items.explanation: The author contrasts prohibition creating a black market with taxing and regulating reducing harm more reliably, favouring regulation over prohibition. The other options reverse or exaggerate the stance.

items.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to INNOVATIVE.
items.explanation: Innovative means introducing new ideas and being original, so creative and new is closest. Traditional, imitative and conservative all point towards keeping old ways.

items.passage: A university must cut its scholarship budget by 20 percent. It can cut awards for all recipients equally, remove scholarships from students with the highest family incomes among recipients, or end scholarships for new entrants while protecting current students. Each option affects a different group.
items.question: Which principle should guide the cut?
options: Protect the students for whom the scholarship most affects the ability to continue studying
Protect the students with the best grades only
Cut the largest scholarships first regardless of need
items.explanation: Protecting students whose continuation depends most on the award targets the cut where it does least educational harm. Cutting by size, grades or lottery ignores need and the purpose of the scholarship.

items.question: Ending scholarships for new entrants while protecting current students is attractive because it
options: avoids breaking a promise to students who planned around the award
items.explanation: Protecting current students honours the reliance they placed on the award when enrolling. It does not increase the budget, help the poorest new applicants, or remove the need to communicate.

items.question: What should the university do before deciding?
options: Choose the option the press will like best
Analyse which recipients would drop out under each option and consult student representatives
Delay the decision until after admissions
items.explanation: Modelling dropout effects under each option and consulting representatives grounds the choice in evidence and legitimacy. Announcing without data, chasing press approval and delaying past admissions all avoid that analysis.

items.passage: A firm adopted a software vendor whose system now holds all its customer data in a proprietary format. Switching vendors would cost a large sum and take a year. The current vendor has raised prices sharply, knowing switching is hard. The firm must decide whether to pay, switch, or negotiate from a weak position.
items.question: What is the firm's best immediate step?
options: Assess the true switching cost, build an exit plan, and negotiate with a credible alternative in hand
items.explanation: A credible exit plan plus a real alternative gives negotiation leverage that paying without question or suing without preparation lacks. Stopping use immediately would disrupt operations before any replacement exists.

items.question: The root mistake was made earlier, when the firm
options: accepted a proprietary format without an exit clause or data portability requirement
items.explanation: Accepting lock-in without exit or portability terms created the vulnerability the vendor now exploits. Choosing a vendor, negotiating price and training staff are normal steps, not the mistake.

items.question: For future vendor contracts, the firm should require
options: A ban on all price increases
A contract that can never be ended
Data export in open formats, exit assistance, and price-change limits
items.explanation: Open-format export, exit assistance and price-change limits directly prevent a repeat of lock-in. Lowest price alone, a ban on increases and an unending contract all create new rigidities or ignore the exit problem.

items.passage: A bank uses an automated system to screen small business loans. A branch manager notices that applications from one neighbourhood are rejected at three times the rate of others, although the applicants have similar incomes and credit histories. The system's vendor says the model is proprietary and cannot be explained. Head office praises the system's speed and wants it rolled out to all branches.
items.question: What should the manager do first?
options: Ask the vendor for a discount on the system
Approve all loans from the affected neighbourhood to compensate
Pause new rejections from the system and review a sample of declined applications manually
Wait for head office to notice the pattern on its own
items.explanation: The manager should stop the harm first by pausing automated rejections and manually reviewing a sample, which establishes whether the pattern is real. Approving everything overcorrects blindly, waiting lets the harm continue, and a discount does not fix the decisions.

items.question: The vendor's refusal to explain the model is a problem because
options: Loan officers prefer paper files to software
The bank remains accountable for decisions it cannot explain, especially when they may be biased
The vendor charges too much for support
The bank's computers are too slow to run the model
items.explanation: Accountability cannot be outsourced. If the bank cannot explain why a loan was refused, it cannot defend the decision, detect bias, or correct errors. Speed of computers, staff preferences and support pricing are beside the point.

items.question: What should the bank require before a wider rollout?
options: A faster server to process applications
A marketing campaign announcing the new system
A bonus for branches that use the system most
A documented fairness test across neighbourhoods and a human review step for rejections
items.explanation: Before scaling, the bank needs evidence that the system treats neighbourhoods fairly and a human check on rejections. Faster servers, marketing and usage bonuses do nothing about the fairness risk.

items.passage: A hospital has one intensive-care bed left and two patients need it. One is a young patient with a high chance of recovery; the other is an older patient who arrived first and has a lower chance of recovery. The hospital's policy says beds go to the first arrival, but the medical team believes the bed would save more life-years if given to the younger patient.
items.question: What is the central conflict in this decision?
options: A first-come rule versus maximising expected benefit
items.explanation: The conflict is between following the first-arrival rule and allocating the bed where expected benefit is greatest. Cost, staff preference and public-private funding are not the core tension described.

items.question: Which process best respects both fairness and clinical judgement?
options: Apply a transparent triage protocol, reviewed by a second clinician, with reasons documented
Allocate by lottery without clinical input
Give the bed to whoever's family argues loudest
Let the senior doctor decide alone without a record
items.explanation: A transparent triage protocol with second review and documented reasons makes the decision checkable and consistent. Solo undocumented choice, family pressure and pure lottery all abandon either fairness or clinical judgement.

items.question: If the hospital follows the first-arrival rule here, it should also
options: Explain the rule honestly and offer the best alternative care available
Hide the reasoning from the second patient's family
Promise the bed will free up soon
items.explanation: Honest explanation of the rule plus the best alternative care respects the family even when the outcome disappoints. Hiding reasons, false promises and blame all damage trust without helping the patient.

items.passage: A fast-food franchisor learns that one franchise outlet is cutting corners on hygiene to save costs. The outlet is in a high-traffic location and generates strong royalties. Closing it will lose revenue and may lead to a legal dispute; warning it privately may not change behaviour.
items.question: What should the franchisor do?
options: Quietly lower the royalty rate to keep the outlet happy
Inspect, require corrective action with a deadline, and suspend or terminate if the outlet fails to comply
Ignore the outlet to protect royalties
items.explanation: Inspection with a deadline and suspension or termination for non-compliance protects customers and the brand while giving the outlet a fair chance to fix the issue. Ignoring, buying compliance and blaming customers all leave the hygiene risk in place.

items.question: The royalty revenue is not a good reason to tolerate the outlet because
options: a hygiene failure at one outlet damages trust in the whole brand, outweighing one outlet's royalties
items.explanation: One outlet's hygiene failure can damage the entire brand's reputation, so the system-wide loss outweighs one outlet's royalties. Royalties matter, franchisees do pay them, and disputes are not cheap.

items.question: What system change would prevent a repeat?
options: Unannounced audits, a clear hygiene standard, and a public reporting route for staff and customers
items.explanation: Unannounced audits, a clear standard and a reporting route make cutting corners harder to hide. Less frequent inspections, higher royalties and fewer outlets do not address detection or standards.

items.passage: A coaching institute learns that a question paper for an upcoming entrance test may have leaked to a small group of students. The institute's own mock tests are unaffected, but its students are anxious. The institute can warn students, report the matter to the test authority, or stay silent to avoid panic.
items.question: What should the institute do?
options: Spread the leaked paper to all students to level the field
Report the information to the test authority with whatever evidence it holds, and tell students factually what is known
items.explanation: Reporting to the authority with evidence gives the body that can act the information it needs, and factual communication calms students without spreading the leak. Silence, spreading the paper and cancelling classes all worsen fairness or anxiety.

items.question: Spreading the leaked paper to level the field is wrong because it
options: widens the leak, rewards wrongdoing, and may itself be unlawful
items.explanation: Spreading the leak expands the unfairness, rewards the leak, and may break the law, rather than restoring fairness. Helping many students does not make an unfair advantage fair, and cost and time are not the issue.

items.question: What should the institute tell its students?
options: That the test is definitely cancelled
Only what is verified, what is being done, and how students should prepare regardless
That the leak is a rumour with no basis
items.explanation: Verified facts, the action being taken, and preparation advice give students something useful without speculation. Definite cancellation, denial and silence all mislead or abandon anxious students.

items.passage: A charity spends 25 percent of donations on administration and fundraising. Donors complain the share is too high. The charity argues the spending funds the systems that let it deliver aid efficiently and that cutting it would reduce total aid delivered. A rival charity spends 10 percent on overhead but delivers far less aid in total.
items.question: Which measure best judges the charity?
options: Total aid delivered per rupee donated and the outcomes achieved
The size of the charity's office
items.explanation: Aid delivered per rupee and outcomes achieved capture what donors actually buy, while overhead percentage alone ignores scale and effectiveness. Office size and donor count do not measure impact.

items.question: The rival charity's lower overhead does not prove it is better because
options: it delivers far less aid in total, so efficiency must be judged against outcomes
items.explanation: Delivering far less aid in total means the lower percentage may reflect smaller scale or weaker delivery, not better use of money. Lower overhead is not always worse and overhead is not irrelevant, but percentage alone cannot settle the comparison.

items.question: What should the charity do about donor concern?
options: Publish a clear breakdown of spending and the outcomes it produces
Cut administration at once without a plan
items.explanation: Publishing a clear breakdown and outcomes lets donors judge value for themselves. Hiding, unplanned cuts and stopping fundraising all avoid the accountability donors are asking for.

items.question: What is 15% of 240?
items.explanation: 15% of 240 is 240 x 15/100 = 36. Ten percent is 24 and five percent is 12, and 24 + 12 = 36, which is a quick check.

items.question: What is the least common multiple of 12 and 18?
items.explanation: Multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36, 48 and of 18 are 18, 36, 54, so the smallest common multiple is 36.

items.question: What is the value of 5^2 + 12^2?
items.explanation: 25 + 144 = 169, which is 13^2, the hypotenuse of the 5-12-13 triangle. Recognising the Pythagorean triple 5-12-13 makes this immediate.

items.question: What is the average of 20, 30, 40 and 50?
items.explanation: The sum is 140 and there are 4 numbers, so the average is 140/4 = 35. The numbers are in arithmetic progression, so the average is also the average of the first and last, (20 + 50)/2 = 35.

items.question: A, B and C share Rs 100 in the ratio 2:3:5. How much does B receive?
items.explanation: The parts total 10, so one part is 100/10 = 10, and B gets 3 x 10 = Rs 30. A gets Rs 20 and C gets Rs 50, and 20 + 30 + 50 = 100, which checks the split.

items.question: Pipe A can fill a tank in 8 hours and pipe B can empty it in 12 hours. If both are opened together, in how many hours will the tank be filled?
items.explanation: A fills 1/8 and B empties 1/12 per hour, so the net rate is 1/8 - 1/12 = 1/24 per hour, giving 24 hours.

items.question: The marked price of an article is Rs 500. If a discount of 10% is given, what is the selling price?
items.explanation: The discount is 10% of 500 = Rs 50, so the selling price is 500 - 50 = Rs 450. The discount is calculated on the marked price, not on the cost price.

items.question: What is the difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on Rs 4000 for 2 years at 5% per annum?
items.explanation: For two years the difference is P x (r/100)^2 = 4000 x 0.0025 = Rs 10. The difference arises because compound interest earns interest on the first year's interest.

items.question: A train 300 metres long running at 72 km/h crosses a 200 metre bridge. How long does it take?
items.explanation: 72 km/h is 20 m/s and the total distance is 300 + 200 = 500 m, so the time is 500/20 = 25 seconds.

items.question: 6 men can complete a job in 12 days. How many days will 4 men take to complete the same job?
items.explanation: The work is 6 x 12 = 72 man-days, so 4 men take 72/4 = 18 days. Fewer men means more days, in inverse proportion, not fewer days.

items.question: If x^2 + 7x + 12 = 0, what is the product of its roots?
items.explanation: The equation factors as (x + 3)(x + 4) = 0, so the roots are -3 and -4, and their product is 12. By the formula, the product is c/a = 12.

items.question: What is the sum of all natural numbers from 1 to 50?
items.explanation: The sum is n(n + 1)/2 = 50 x 51/2 = 1275. Pairing 1 with 50, 2 with 49, and so on gives 25 pairs of 51, which is the same total.

items.question: A die is thrown once. What is the probability of getting an even number?
items.explanation: The even outcomes are 2, 4 and 6, which is 3 of the 6 equally likely outcomes, so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2.

items.question: A triangle has base 10 cm and height 12 cm. What is its area?
items.explanation: Area is (1/2) x base x height = 0.5 x 10 x 12 = 60 sq cm. Doubling the triangle to a rectangle of 10 by 12 gives 120, and half of that is 60.

items.question: What is the remainder when 5^2026 is divided by 4?
items.explanation: Modulo 4, 5 is 1, and 1 raised to any power is 1, so the remainder is 1. Any power of a number congruent to 1 modulo 4 is itself congruent to 1.

items.question: In how many ways can the letters A, B, C, D be arranged if A must come first?
items.explanation: With A fixed in the first position, the remaining three letters can be arranged in 3! = 6 ways.

items.question: A triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. What is its area?
items.explanation: Since 6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10^2, the triangle is right-angled with legs 6 and 8, so its area is (1/2) x 6 x 8 = 24 sq cm.

items.question: If x - 1/x = 4, what is the value of x^2 + 1/x^2?
items.explanation: Squaring gives x^2 - 2 + 1/x^2 = 16, so x^2 + 1/x^2 = 18. The cross term is -2 here because of the minus sign, so it is added back to 16.

items.question: A and B start towards each other from two towns 160 km apart. A travels at 50 km/h and B at 30 km/h. After how long do they meet?
items.explanation: Their closing speed is 50 + 30 = 80 km/h, so they meet after 160/80 = 2 hours. When two bodies move towards each other, their speeds add.

items.question: A vessel contains 50 litres of solution with 40% acid. How much pure acid must be added to make the acid 50% of the solution?
items.explanation: The solution has 20 litres of acid and 30 litres of water. Adding x litres of acid gives (20 + x)/(50 + x) = 1/2, so 40 + 2x = 50 + x, giving x = 10 litres.

items.question: What is the value of log2(32) + log2(2)?
items.explanation: log2(32) is 5 because 2^5 = 32, and log2(2) is 1, so the sum is 6. The sum of two logs of the same base is the log of the product, and 32 x 2 = 64 = 2^6.

items.question: What is the volume of a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 7 cm? (Use pi = 22/7)
items.explanation: Volume is pi x r^2 x h = (22/7) x 9 x 7 = 22 x 9 = 198 cubic cm. The 7 in the height cancels the 7 in the denominator of pi, keeping the arithmetic clean.

items.question: Which factory had the highest total production over the four quarters?

diagram.caption: Production (units) of four factories, Q1 to Q4

items.explanation: Adding the four quarters: F1 = 520, F2 = 600, F3 = 380, F4 = 505. Factory F2 has the highest total at 600 units.

items.question: What is the percentage growth in Factory F1's production from Q1 to Q4?
items.explanation: Factory F1's production rose from 100 units in Q1 to 160 units in Q4, an increase of 60 units. The percentage growth is 60/100 x 100 = 60%.

items.question: In which quarter was the combined production of all four factories the highest, and by how much did it exceed the lowest quarter?
items.explanation: The combined totals are Q1 = 450, Q2 = 455, Q3 = 540 and Q4 = 560 units. The highest is Q4 at 560 and the lowest is Q1 at 450, so Q4 exceeds Q1 by 110 units.

items.question: What is the overall percentage increase in total revenue from 2023 to 2024?

diagram.caption: Revenue (Rs crore) of four regions, 2023 and 2024

items.explanation: Total revenue in 2023 was Rs 900 crore and in 2024 it was Rs 1055 crore. The increase is 155 on a base of 900, which is 17.2%.

items.question: Which region recorded the highest percentage growth in revenue?
items.explanation: Growth rates are: North 20.0%, South 24.0%, East 10.0%, West 10.0%. South has the highest percentage growth at 24.0%.

items.question: What is the ratio of North region revenue to South region revenue in 2024?
items.explanation: In 2024 North had Rs 360 crore and South had Rs 310 crore, so the ratio is 360:310. Dividing both sides by 10 gives 36:31.

items.question: Which is the tallest mountain in the world?
items.explanation: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain in the world at 8,849 metres. K2 is second, Kangchenjunga third, and Kilimanjaro is the tallest in Africa.

items.question: What is the national bird of India?
items.explanation: The Indian peafowl is the national bird of India. The sparrow is common but not the national bird, the eagle is the national bird of the United States, and the owl is associated with Lakshmi.

items.question: Which city is home to the Taj Mahal?
items.explanation: The Taj Mahal is in Agra, Uttar Pradesh. Delhi has the Red Fort and Qutub Minar, Jaipur has the Hawa Mahal, and Lucknow is known for the Bara Imambara.

items.question: Who was the first Indian to win a Nobel Prize?
items.explanation: Rabindranath Tagore won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913, the first Indian to win a Nobel. C V Raman won in Physics in 1930, Mother Teresa won the Peace Prize in 1979, and Amartya Sen won in Economics in 1998.

items.question: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
items.explanation: The symbol for gold is Au, from the Latin word aurum. Ag is silver, Gd is gadolinium, and Go is not an element symbol.

items.question: Which is the longest river in the world?
items.explanation: The Nile is the longest river in the world at about 6,650 km. The Amazon carries more water, the Yangtze is the longest in Asia, and the Mississippi is the longest in North America.

items.question: Which gas is released by plants at night?
items.explanation: At night, without sunlight for photosynthesis, plants respire and release carbon dioxide. During the day they release oxygen, while nitrogen and hydrogen are not released as gases by plants.

items.question: The headquarters of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is located in which city?
items.explanation: ASEAN is headquartered in Jakarta, Indonesia. Bangkok is the capital of Thailand, Singapore is a member state, and Kuala Lumpur is the capital of Malaysia.

items.question: Who wrote 'The God of Small Things'?
items.explanation: Arundhati Roy wrote 'The God of Small Things' and won the Booker Prize for it in 1997. Jhumpa Lahiri wrote 'Interpreter of Maladies', Kiran Desai wrote 'The Inheritance of Loss', and Anita Desai wrote 'Clear Light of Day'.

items.question: Which Indian state is the smallest by area?
items.explanation: Goa is the smallest Indian state by area, about 3,702 sq km. Sikkim is second smallest, Tripura is third, and Mizoram is larger than all three.

items.question: Which article of the Indian Constitution provides for the Finance Commission?
items.explanation: Article 280 provides for the Finance Commission, which recommends the sharing of taxes between the Union and the states. Article 270 deals with taxes levied by the Union, and Article 275 with grants-in-aid.

items.question: The Dandi March was led by Mahatma Gandhi in which year?
items.explanation: The Dandi March, or Salt March, began in March 1930. The Non-Cooperation Movement began in 1920, the Quit India Movement in 1942, and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre happened in 1919.

items.question: Who is best known for the theory of evolution by natural selection?
items.explanation: Charles Darwin published 'On the Origin of Species' in 1859, setting out evolution by natural selection. Mendel founded genetics, Lamarck proposed inheritance of acquired traits, and Pasteur worked on germs and vaccines.

items.question: Which is the largest producer of wheat in India?
items.explanation: Uttar Pradesh is the largest producer of wheat in India. Punjab is second, Haryana third, and Madhya Pradesh is a smaller wheat producer.

items.question: The headquarters of the Asian Development Bank is located in which city?
items.explanation: The Asian Development Bank is headquartered in Manila, Philippines. Tokyo hosts the Bank of Japan, Beijing hosts the AIIB, and Bangkok hosts UNESCAP.

items.question: Who was the first woman Chief Minister of India?
items.explanation: Sucheta Kripalani became Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh in 1963, the first woman to head a state government in India. Indira Gandhi was Prime Minister, Mayawati was a later UP Chief Minister, and Anandiben Patel led Gujarat.

items.question: Which amendment is known as the 'Mini Constitution'?
items.explanation: The 42nd Amendment of 1976 is called the Mini Constitution because it made sweeping changes to the Constitution. The 44th Amendment reversed some of them, the 52nd added the anti-defection law, and the 86th introduced the right to education.

items.question: Which Indian won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930?
items.explanation: C V Raman won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930 for the Raman Effect. Homi Bhabha founded India's atomic energy programme, Bose worked on quantum statistics, and Saha worked on astrophysics.

items.question: Which committee recommended the three-tier Panchayati Raj system in India?
items.explanation: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee of 1957 recommended the three-tier Panchayati Raj system. The Ashok Mehta Committee reviewed it in 1977, the Sarkaria Commission dealt with Centre-state relations, and the Narasimham Committee dealt with banking.

items.question: The 42nd Amendment added which words to the Preamble of the Indian Constitution?
items.explanation: The 42nd Amendment of 1976 added the words Socialist, Secular and Integrity to the Preamble. Sovereign and Democratic, Justice and Liberty, and Fraternity and Equality were already in the original Preamble.

items.question: Who founded the Indian National Congress?
items.explanation: Allan Octavian Hume, a retired British civil servant, founded the Indian National Congress in 1885. Dadabhai Naoroji was its early president, Gokhale was a later leader, and Banerjee founded the Indian National Association.

items.question: Which is the deepest lake in the world?
items.explanation: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake in the world, over 1,600 metres deep. The Caspian Sea is the largest lake by area, Tanganyika is the second deepest, and Great Slave Lake is the deepest in North America.

items.question: The 'Doha Round' of negotiations relates to which organisation?
items.explanation: The Doha Round is a round of trade negotiations under the World Trade Organization, launched in 2001. The IMF deals with monetary stability, the World Bank with development lending, and the UN is a general body.

items.question: Who is known as the 'Father of the Indian Space Programme'?
items.explanation: Vikram Sarabhai founded INCOSPAR, the predecessor of ISRO, and is called the Father of the Indian Space Programme. Homi Bhabha founded the atomic energy programme, Satish Dhawan led ISRO, and Kalam worked on missiles and space launch vehicles.

items.question: Which battle is considered the beginning of British rule in India?
items.explanation: The Battle of Plassey in 1757 is considered the beginning of British rule in India. Buxar in 1764 consolidated it, Panipat was fought between Indian rulers, and Wandiwash in 1760 ended French power in India.
